edges.description: Effector-derived TNF drives accumulation of pro-inflammatory monocyte-derived macrophages at the tumour site and induces host IL-6 and IL-1 beta, making this edge the link between the engineered cell and the host amplifier.
Myeloid cytokine output escapes local control and becomes the systemic cytokine elevation that produces the clinical syndrome.
The cytokines that activate endothelium rise with the severity of the neurological arm, which is the measured link between systemic cytokine concentration and endothelial activation.
Fever is the obligatory presenting sign and rises with the cytokine elevation; in the mouse model, effector-mediated tumour clearance produced fever together with elevated IL-6.
The same endothelial process extends to the cerebral microvasculature, where loss of barrier function admits systemic cytokines to the cerebrospinal fluid.

nodes.description: A proposed mechanism for the neurological arm. Increased blood-brain barrier permeability admits high concentrations of systemic cytokines to the cerebrospinal fluid; interferon gamma and tumour necrosis factor then stress brain vascular pericytes, which secrete interleukin-6 and vascular endothelial growth factor and further increase barrier permeability. This is a candidate account rather than a settled one. The consensus panel states that the neurotoxicity syndrome has unclear pathophysiology, distinct from CRS, and that it does not usually respond to IL-6 receptor blockade, so the mechanism here is not simply the systemic one acting in the brain.

nodes.description: The initiating event is engagement of target antigen by an infused or redirected immune effector cell. Signalling through the chimeric antigen receptor, or through a bispecific antibody bridging the effector cell to its target, drives effector cell proliferation, cytokine secretion and target cell lysis. The magnitude of this engagement scales with antigen burden and with infused cell dose. Host properties matter too: pre-existing neurological comorbidity was an independent risk factor for the neurological arm in multivariable analysis, so this node is not the only determinant of severity.

nodes.description: Activated effector cells secrete tumour necrosis factor. This is an upstream signal of the syndrome rather than one of its dominant mediators: it acts on the host myeloid compartment, which then supplies the interleukin-1 and interleukin-6 that produce the systemic illness. Selective disruption of effector-derived TNF in a mouse model reduces macrophage accumulation and host cytokine induction and changes CRS severity, which places TNF upstream of the myeloid amplifier. Interferon gamma and GM-CSF are also described as effector cytokines in CRS, and interferon gamma is measured at high concentration in serum and cerebrospinal fluid, but none of the sources cited here attributes its production to the effector cells specifically, so no such process is bound on this node.

nodes.description: Circulating cytokines act on vascular endothelium throughout the body. Activated endothelium releases von Willebrand factor and angiopoietin-2 from Weibel-Palade bodies, loses barrier integrity and becomes procoagulant, so capillary leak and consumptive coagulopathy appear together. Endothelial activation is detectable early, before the most severe manifestations, and baseline markers of it identify patients at higher risk.

nodes.description: Host monocytes and macrophages, not the engineered effector cells, are the major source of the interleukin-1 and interleukin-6 that drive the syndrome. In a humanised mouse model recapitulating CRS, depleting monocytes prevented the syndrome altogether. This node is why an IL-6 receptor antagonist and an IL-1 receptor antagonist both work on the syndrome, and why neither acts on the infused product.

nodes.description: A single dose of tocilizumab given before the first step-up dose of a T-cell-engaging bispecific antibody, to prevent CRS rather than treat it. This is a different clinical claim from reactive tocilizumab above: it is the point where IL-6 receptor blockade has been shown to lower CRS incidence. The evidence comes from bispecific-treated relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma, not CAR-T, and from cohort and single-arm studies rather than randomised trials; the meta-analysis authors call for prospective randomised studies. A reduction in grade 2 or higher CRS did not reach significance in the pooled analysis.
